title: How does JPA/Spring Data auditing with @CreatedDate and @LastModifiedDate differ from Hibernate Envers @Audited history tables?

s1_definition.profdef: Spring Data JPA auditing uses `@CreatedDate`, `@LastModifiedDate`, `@CreatedBy`, and `@LastModifiedBy` with an `AuditingEntityListener` to stamp WHO and WHEN on the current row — it tracks only the latest state. Hibernate Envers `@Audited` goes further: it maintains full revision history in separate audit tables, recording every version of an entity over time so you can query the state of an entity at any past revision.
s1_definition.analogy: Spring Data auditing is like National Bank of India writing "last updated by Priya on 23-Oct, created by Rajesh on 1-Jan" in the margin of the current passbook page — you see when and who last touched it, but not the history. Hibernate Envers is like keeping a photocopy of the passbook every single time anything changes, filed in a separate archive room. With Envers you can pull up exactly what Rajesh's balance was on any date in the past and who changed it.
s1_definition.oneliner: @CreatedDate/@LastModifiedDate stamp the current row; Envers @Audited keeps the full version history.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Spring Data JPA auditing uses `@CreatedDate`, `@LastModifiedDate`, `@CreatedBy`, and `@LastModifiedBy` with an `AuditingEntityListener` to stamp WHO and WHEN on the current row — it tracks only the latest state. Hibernate Envers `@Audited` goes further: it maintains full revision history in separate audit tables, recording every version of an entity over time so you can query the state of an entity at any past revision.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Spring Data auditing is like National Bank of India writing "last updated by Priya on 23-Oct, created by Rajesh on 1-Jan" in the margin of the current passbook page — you see when and who last touched it, but not the history. Hibernate Envers is like keeping a photocopy of the passbook every single time anything changes, filed in a separate archive room. With Envers you can pull up exactly what Rajesh's balance was on any date in the past and who changed it.

**One line to remember:** @CreatedDate/@LastModifiedDate stamp the current row; Envers @Audited keeps the full version history.

sections.s2_technical:
Spring Data auditing requires `@EnableJpaAuditing` on a config class and `@EntityListeners(AuditingEntityListener.class)` on the entity. Then fields annotated `@CreatedDate` and `@LastModifiedDate` are filled automatically. For example, on Priya's account, `@LastModifiedDate private Instant updatedAt` is set to now on every update. For WHO, `@CreatedBy private String createdBy` needs an `AuditorAware` bean that returns the current username, typically from Spring Security.

Envers is activated by adding `hibernate-envers` and annotating an entity `@Audited`. Hibernate then creates `accounts_AUD` and a `REVINFO` table. Every insert, update, or delete writes a revision row. You query history with `AuditReader`: `AuditReaderFactory.get(em).find(Account.class, "SAV2001", revisionNumber)` returns the account as it looked at that revision.

The key difference is scope. Spring Data auditing is cheap and keeps only four extra columns on the same table — it answers "when was this last changed and by whom." Envers is heavier (extra tables, extra inserts on every change) but answers "show me every version and let me reconstruct any past state." In banking, regulators often require full audit trails, which is where Envers shines.

Senior nuance: Envers stores a revision per transaction, and you can add custom revision entity fields (IP address, request id) via a `RevisionListener`. Spring Data auditing can coexist with Envers — use the former for convenient current-row stamps and the latter for the compliance history table.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — When an account record changes, National Bank of India must know when it was created and when it was last modified, plus who did it. This is exactly Spring Data auditing — automatic timestamps and user stamps on the current row.

Problem 2 — A regulator asks: "Show us Rajesh's exact account balance and status as it stood on 15th March, and who changed it that day." Current-row stamps cannot answer this because old values are overwritten. This is exactly Hibernate Envers — a full revision history in audit tables that lets you reconstruct any past state.

We will build an Account entity with both Spring Data auditing fields and Envers @Audited, an AuditorAware bean, and a HistoryService that reads past revisions.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run
java -jar target/account-audit-service-1.0.0.jar

# Change balance a few times, then read history
curl "http://localhost:8080/api/v1/accounts/SAV2001/revisions"
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input: create SAV2001 at 1,000,000, then update balance to 900,000, then to 850,000.

Step 1 — On create, Spring Data auditing sets createdAt, createdBy="teller-priya", updatedAt, updatedBy. Envers writes revision 1 to accounts_AUD with revtype=0 (ADD) and balance 1,000,000.

Step 2 — First update to 900,000 overwrites the current row's balance and updatedAt. Envers writes revision 2 (revtype=1 MOD) with balance 900,000, keeping revision 1 intact.

Step 3 — Second update to 850,000 overwrites again. Envers writes revision 3 with balance 850,000.

Step 4 — `revisionsOf("SAV2001")` returns [1,2,3]. `accountAtRevision("SAV2001", 1)` reconstructs the original 1,000,000 state even though the current row shows 850,000.

```
INFO  Created SAV2001 by teller-priya
Hibernate: insert into accounts_AUD (rev,revtype,...) values (1,0,...)
Hibernate: insert into accounts_AUD (rev,revtype,...) values (2,1,...)
Hibernate: insert into accounts_AUD (rev,revtype,...) values (3,1,...)
INFO  Account SAV2001 at revision 1 had balance 1000000
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Update: PUT /accounts/SAV2001 {"balance":900000}
    │
    ▼
  AccountService (@Transactional)
    │ acc.setBalance(900000)
    ▼
  Hibernate flush
    ├─ Spring Data auditing ──→ updatedAt=now, updatedBy=teller-priya
    │                           (overwrites current row)
    └─ Envers listener ───────→ INSERT accounts_AUD rev=2 revtype=MOD
                                (keeps rev=1 intact)
    │
    ▼
  Current row: SAV2001 balance=900000
  History: rev1=1,000,000  rev2=900,000

  Query path:
    GET /at-revision/1 ──→ AuditReader.find() ──→ reconstruct 1,000,000
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — JPA Auditing vs Envers ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns ──────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Observer: AuditingEntityListener + Envers listener  │
  │   react to lifecycle events (no code in service)    │
  │ Strategy: AuditorAware picks "who" at runtime       │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID ────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ S: HistoryService only reads revisions              │
  │ O: add Envers to an entity by one @Audited, no code │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌───────────────────────────────┐
  │          Account              │
  │  @CreatedDate createdAt       │ current-row stamp
  │  @LastModifiedDate updatedAt  │
  │  @Audited (class-level)       │ full history
  └──────────────┬────────────────┘
                 │ listened by
      ┌──────────┴───────────┐
      ▼                      ▼
  ┌────────────────────┐ ┌────────────────────┐
  │AuditingEntityListener│ │ Envers listener    │
  │ sets created/updated │ │ writes _AUD rows   │
  └────────────────────┘ └────────────────────┘

  ── State Diagram: revision history ──
  [rev1 ADD 1,000,000] → [rev2 MOD 900,000] → [rev3 MOD 850,000]
     (each rev immutable; current row only shows latest)

  ── Call Chain ──
  1. Controller.history() → HistoryService.accountAtRevision(id,1)
  2.   AuditReaderFactory.get(em)
  3.   reader.find(Account, id, 1) → reconstruct past state
  4. return Account@rev1
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
There are two layers of auditing in JPA and they answer different questions. Spring Data auditing uses the annotations CreatedDate, LastModifiedDate, CreatedBy, and LastModifiedBy together with an AuditingEntityListener and the EnableJpaAuditing switch. It stamps when a row was created and last changed, and who did it, directly onto the current row. It is cheap, adds only a handful of columns, and answers "when was this last touched and by whom." For the who part I provide an AuditorAware bean that pulls the username from the security context.

Hibernate Envers is a different tool for a different need. By adding the Audited annotation and the Envers dependency, Hibernate maintains full revision history in separate audit tables, one suffixed AUD per entity plus a shared REVINFO table. Every insert, update, and delete writes a revision row, so I can use an AuditReader to reconstruct exactly what an entity looked like at any past revision. The trade-off is that Envers is heavier because it writes extra rows on every change and stores the entire history.

In our National Bank of India system I use both together. The current account row carries created and updated stamps so support staff can see at a glance when it last changed, and Envers keeps the compliance history so that when a regulator asks what Rajesh's balance and status were on a specific date and who changed them, I can answer precisely by reading the revision that was active on that date. Banking regulations frequently mandate multi-year audit trails, and current-row stamps simply cannot satisfy that because old values are overwritten.

The senior nuance I raise is extensibility and retention. With Envers I can attach a custom revision entity via a RevisionListener to capture the request id, IP address, or channel alongside each revision, which is invaluable for forensic investigations. And because the audit tables grow forever, I plan a retention and archival strategy, exporting old revisions to cold storage like S3 so the operational database stays lean while still meeting the seven-year retention banks typically require.

---

keyPoints: Hibernate Envers @Audited: full audit trail — stores every version
